title: Memorandum of Contract for Real Estate Wholesaling: What It Is and Why You Need One
excerpt: A memorandum of contract is one of the most powerful legal tools a wholesaler can use to protect a deal before it closes. Learn how it works, when to file it, and how to use it to keep sellers from backing out.

sections.content: You locked up a great deal. The seller signed the purchase agreement, you shook hands, and now you are hunting for a buyer. Then your phone rings. The seller says they changed their mind — or worse, they already signed a new contract with someone else. If you never filed a memorandum of contract, you may have very little legal recourse. This one simple document, often just one page long, can save your entire deal.
What Is a Memorandum of Contract in Real Estate Wholesaling?

A memorandum of contract — also called a memorandum of agreement, notice of interest, or short form memorandum — is a brief legal document that summarizes the key terms of your purchase and sale agreement without disclosing the full price or all the details. Once signed and notarized, you record it with the county recorder's office in the county where the property sits. This creates what lawyers call a 'cloud on title,' which means no other buyer can close on that property without first dealing with your recorded interest. Think of it as planting a legal flag on the property the moment your contract is signed.
In wholesaling, your contract is your asset. If you don't protect it, you don't really own anything.
Why Wholesalers Should Always Use a Memorandum of Contract

Most new wholesalers skip this step because it feels like extra paperwork. But experienced investors — especially those doing deals in competitive markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) — know it is non-negotiable. Here is why filing this document matters so much.

items: Prevents sellers from accepting a higher offer from another buyer while you are marketing the deal
Stops the seller from refinancing or taking out a new loan using the property as collateral
Provides proof of your equitable interest in the property if a dispute goes to court
Signals to any title company or closing attorney that your agreement must be satisfied before the property transfers
Creates a paper trail showing the date your contract was executed

sections.content: File your memorandum of contract the same day your seller signs your purchase agreement — not tomorrow, not after you find a buyer. Recording fees are usually between $15 and $50, and the protection you get is worth far more than that on any deal with profit potential.
What Should a Memorandum of Contract Include?

The memorandum does not need to be complicated. In fact, keeping it short is intentional — you do not want to reveal your purchase price or assignment fee to the world. At a minimum, your memorandum should include the following information.

items: Full legal names of the buyer (you or your LLC) and the seller
The complete legal description of the property, as it appears on the deed
The property address and parcel number
The effective date of the purchase and sale agreement
The expiration date or closing deadline of the contract
A statement that you hold equitable interest in the property
Notarized signatures from both the buyer and the seller

sections.content: Notice what is NOT listed above: the purchase price. This is deliberate. Omitting the price keeps your deal structure private, prevents future buyers from knowing your spread, and keeps nosy neighbors or competing investors out of your business. Check your state's specific requirements, as a handful of states have unique formatting rules for recorded documents.
Step-by-Step: How to File a Memorandum of Contract
Step 1 — Prepare the Memorandum Immediately After Contract Signing

Draft your memorandum as soon as your seller signs the purchase agreement. Many wholesalers use a template their real estate attorney reviewed in advance. You can also have the seller sign both the purchase agreement and the memorandum at the same time, since both documents require signatures.
Step 2 — Get It Notarized

Most county recorders require notarized signatures before a document can be officially recorded. You can find a notary at most banks, shipping stores, or through online notary platforms for around $5 to $25. Some real estate attorneys include notarization in their consultation fee.
Step 3 — Record It at the County Recorder's Office

Take the notarized document to the county recorder's office — or in some counties, the clerk of court — in the county where the property is located. Pay the recording fee, typically between $15 and $75 depending on your state and the number of pages. You will receive a stamped copy with a recording date. That date is your official protection date.
Step 4 — Release the Memorandum After the Deal Closes or Falls Through

Once your deal closes, the title company will typically handle releasing the memorandum as part of the closing process. If the deal falls through and you decide not to pursue it, you must file a release or cancellation of the memorandum. Failing to do so is both unprofessional and potentially illegal. Always clean up recorded documents you no longer need.
Common Mistakes Wholesalers Make With Memorandums

items: Waiting too long to file — even 24 hours can allow another transaction to record first
Using an incorrect or incomplete legal property description, which can make the recording invalid
Forgetting to release the memorandum after a deal dies, which can create legal liability
Recording in the wrong county when a property sits near a county line
Trying to use the memorandum as a substitute for a solid, legally binding purchase agreement

Does a Memorandum of Contract Work for Assignment Deals?

Yes — and it is just as important for assignment deals as it is for double closings. When you assign a contract, you are transferring your equitable interest to an end buyer. That interest only exists if you actually have a valid, enforceable contract. Recording a memorandum proves your interest is real and on the public record. If the seller tries to get out of the deal after you have already lined up a cash buyer, your recorded memorandum gives you legal standing to enforce the original agreement or pursue damages. This is especially valuable on deals where your assignment fee is $10,000 or more.

Before you spend time marketing a deal to buyers, run your numbers first. State-Specific Considerations to Know

Laws around memorandums of contract vary by state. In some states like Florida and Georgia, recording memorandums is a common, widely accepted practice. In others, sellers may push back or be unfamiliar with the document, which is why your explanation matters. In Texas, the process may differ slightly due to the state's unique property recording system. Always work with a local real estate attorney to get a template that is compliant with your state's recording statutes. The cost of a one-hour legal consultation is a small price compared to losing a $15,000 wholesale deal because of a documentation error.
